name: Chemical peels (TCA, Jessner)

card.summary: Medium-depth acid peels, using trichloroacetic acid alone or after Jessner's solution, used by clinicians for photoaging, pigment and scars; DIY versions carry higher injury risk.
card.aka: TCA peel, Jessner's peel, Jessner's + TCA, medium-depth peel
card.note: Medium-depth peels are described as clinician-performed procedures; pigment changes and scarring are the main risks, and DIY kits carry higher risk.

quick.overview:
A medium-depth chemical peel uses a caustic acid to injure the upper skin layers in a controlled way so that new skin forms. Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is the usual agent, and Jessner's solution is often applied first to make the TCA act more evenly.

Dermatology papers describe them for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses, fine wrinkles, melasma and acne scars. On looksmax.org a small number of members have discussed doing TCA peels at home, but those threads provide no usable evidence.
quick.mechanism: TCA denatures proteins in the skin, causing a controlled injury and shedding followed by regeneration. Jessner's solution (a keratolytic mix) is used beforehand in the Jessner plus TCA technique, and glycolic acid has also been used as a pre-treatment so that TCA penetrates more predictably.
quick.risks: Reported risks include prolonged redness, photosensitivity, pigment changes, milia, atrophy and scarring. A general reference states that deeper peels bring more complications and that DIY kits carry higher risk of injury and scarring. Tretinoin pre-treatment has been shown in one trial to accelerate healing.

lead: Medium-depth chemical peels use trichloroacetic acid (TCA), sometimes in combination with Jessner's solution or glycolic acid, to produce a controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis. They are used in dermatology for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses, wrinkles, pigmentary disorders such as melasma and benign lesions, and atrophic acne scars.[1][2][3][4]

A 1989 paper described the Jessner's plus TCA peel as a medium-depth peel for photoaging, actinic keratoses and rhytides, and a 1994 paper described a glycolic acid plus TCA variant intended to make penetration more predictable.[1][5] A 1999 report described a standardised TCA-based peel with depth control.[6]

General references state that medium-depth peels must be performed by a medical provider and that deeper peels bring more complications.[7] Published studies in the area are mostly small clinical series, comparisons and some randomised trials.

paras: Peels are classed by depth: light peels use alpha- or beta-hydroxy acids, medium peels use TCA, and deep peels have historically used phenol with croton oil.[7] TCA peels are performed in an office or outpatient setting, patients often feel warmth or burning, and sedation or topical anaesthetic is sometimes used.[7][9]

The Jessner's plus TCA technique applies Jessner's solution before TCA, and an approach published in 1994 used 70 percent glycolic acid, diluted after two minutes, before 35 percent TCA.[1][5] The 1999 blue peel is a standardised variant intended to control depth.[6]

A review of the Jessner's plus TCA peel describes it as an enhanced medium-depth peel for photoaged skin.[10] A study of combination therapy used subcision, microneedling and a 15 percent TCA peel in 50 patients with atrophic acne scars.[3]

For pigment, a comparative study examined TCA peel with and without topical ascorbic acid in melasma, and a 2004 paper described a focal TCA peel method for benign pigmented lesions in dark-skinned patients.[8][4]

Chemical peels date to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities. Phenol-croton oil peeling entered mainstream practice in the 1960s.[7] The Jessner's plus TCA method was published in 1989.[1]

General references list photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin atrophy, texture changes and scarring as risks, and state that DIY kits carry a higher risk of injury and scarring.[7] A trial found that tretinoin pre-treatment accelerated healing after TCA peel.[2]
A 2000 comparison examined two topical anaesthetic creams for pain relief in medium-depth peeling.[9]

Medium-depth peels are discussed in hardmaxxing contexts as clinic-based options for pigment and texture. Looksmax.org contains at least one thread in which members ask who has done a DIY TCA peel; the retrievable posts do not describe outcomes and are not cited here.

A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised study in 16 men (mean age 67) with actinically damaged skin applied 0.1 percent tretinoin and placebo to opposite sides for 14 days before a 35 percent TCA peel to assess healing.[2] Case series and comparative studies cover Jessner plus TCA for photoaging, glycolic acid plus TCA, and TCA in melasma and acne scars.[1][3][5][8]

Registered trials include a completed phase 4 comparison of Jessner's solution versus TCA for melasma (2008, n=19), a completed phase 4 study of 15 percent TCA for hand lentigines (2023, n=20) and a phase 4 trial combining TCA with microdermabrasion for melasma (2021, n=60, status unknown).[11][12][13] A 2023 paper used high-frequency ultrasound to monitor anti-aging skin therapy.[14] Outcome data from the registrations are not summarised here.

timeline.event: Jessner's plus TCA medium-depth peel described.[1]
Randomised trial of tretinoin pre-treatment before TCA peel.[2]
Glycolic acid plus TCA peel described.[5]
TCA-based blue peel with depth control described.[6]
